q: The Stroop effect demonstrates interference in:

concept.t: In the Stroop task you name the ink colour of a colour word (RED printed in blue). Automatic word reading cannot be filtered out, so it interferes.
The task shows a failure of selective attention: you cannot screen out the irrelevant word. No stored memory is being retrieved or rehearsed.

wrong.a: Recovering stored facts or events; a memory distractor, since nothing is retrieved from storage in the task.
wrong.b: Briefly holding and rehearsing information; a memory distractor, since nothing is rehearsed, the clash is between word and ink.
wrong.d: Memory for skills and habits, like riding a bike; a memory distractor, since the task tests attention, not a stored skill.

q: Which psychological process is the Stroop effect most closely associated with?

concept.t: The colours and words are perceived perfectly well. The difficulty lies in selecting the relevant dimension (ink colour) and inhibiting the automatic one (the word).
Selecting one input and inhibiting another is the job of attention, so the Stroop effect is an attention effect.

wrong.a: No stored item has to be recalled; the conflict arises while naming a colour that is in front of you.
wrong.c: Tempting, but the colours and words are perceived perfectly well; the problem is choosing which one to respond to.
wrong.d: Reading skill matters (the word is read automatically), but the effect is not about how language develops.

q: In cognitive psychology, the "Stroop effect" primarily demonstrates which cognitive phenomenon?

concept.t: When a colour word and its ink colour conflict (BLUE printed in red), the two sources of information compete and reaction time slows.
The Stroop effect is this interference: slower naming on conflicting trials than on matching or neutral ones.

wrong.b: Describes semantic priming or organisation effects in memory, not interference between word and colour.
wrong.c: False: dividing attention reduces accuracy rather than increasing it.
wrong.d: Belongs to memory research on schemas and episodic recall, not to the Stroop task.

q: "Stroop effect" is an account of:

concept.t: Each Stroop stimulus has two dimensions: the printed word and its ink colour. One dimension, the word, dominates the other in controlling the response.
One stimulus attribute overpowering another is what stimulus dominance names, and it is the keyed answer.

wrong.b: Tempts because the word is meaningful, but the keyed answer describes one stimulus attribute overpowering another, not meaning as such.
wrong.c: Not a term used for this effect; the dominance is between two attributes of the stimulus, not the instructions.
wrong.d: Not a term used for this effect; the competing attributes are a word and a colour, not concepts.

q: Air traffic controllers and radar readers provide us with a good example of which of the following phenomena?

concept.t: Sustained attention, or vigilance, is watching for rare, unpredictable signals over long periods.
The classic lab task is the Mackworth clock, where a pointer occasionally makes a double jump the observer must catch. Radar readers and air traffic controllers face the same demand.

wrong.a: Picks one input among several; the controller's main problem is staying alert for rare signals, not filtering.
wrong.c: Handles two tasks at once; the defining demand here is long-duration monitoring.
wrong.d: Not a standard term in attention research; perception is involved, but the named phenomenon is vigilance.

q: Why do the number plates of motorbikes and cars carry only four-digit numbers coupled with some letters?

concept.t: Span of attention is the number of items that can be apprehended at a glance: about six to eight, fewer for accuracy.
So number plates use short groups (four digits plus some letters) that an observer can take in quickly in one look.

wrong.a: Choosing one input over others; it explains focusing on a plate, not why the plate's length is limited.
wrong.c: Doing two things at once; plate design is about how much fits in one glance, not task sharing.
wrong.d: Staying vigilant over long periods; a glance at a passing plate is brief, not prolonged.

q: Who developed the filter-attenuation theory?

concept.t: Treisman (1964) modified Broadbent's all-or-none filter into an attenuator: unattended messages are turned down, not blocked.
Weakened messages can still get through if they matter, which is why the theory is called filter-attenuation.

wrong.a: Proposed the original all-or-none filter (1958); Treisman revised it, so naming him is the trap.
wrong.c: With Heinz, proposed the multimode theory (1978), in which the point of selection is flexible.
wrong.d: Co-author with Johnston of the multimode theory (1978), not the attenuation theory.

q: You are at a party and someone calls out your name. Instantly, in the middle of a crowd, you can hear it. This phenomenon is called:

concept.t: The cocktail party phenomenon is picking out your own name from a conversation you were not attending to. Named after Cherry (1953) and shown in the lab by Moray (1959).
Treisman's low-threshold dictionary units explain it: personally important words like your name need very little signal to be recognised.

wrong.a: Refers to the narrow stage in attention models where processing is limited, not to this effect.
wrong.c: Handling two tasks at once; hearing your name is an unattended message breaking through, not deliberate sharing.
wrong.d: Staying vigilant over long periods; the name is noticed instantly, without prolonged watching.

q: What term describes the phenomenon where individuals fail to notice significant changes in their environment, even when those changes are obvious?
who: Rensink and colleagues; Simons and Levin

concept.t: The stem stresses changes, which points to change blindness: failing to notice that something in a scene has changed.
Rensink and colleagues showed it with flickering pictures; in Simons and Levin's door study, people missed that the stranger they were talking to had been swapped.

wrong.b: Missing an unexpected object altogether (as in the gorilla study); the stem is about changes, not a new object.
wrong.c: The stable perception of objects; a perceptual achievement, not a failure to notice.
wrong.d: The general process of focusing on some inputs; it underlies change blindness but is not the term for it.

q: Low-prejudiced people engage in:

concept.t: In Devine's (1989) model, stereotypes are activated automatically in everyone, high- or low-prejudiced.
Low-prejudiced people use controlled, effortful processing to override the activated stereotype, so they refute it.

wrong.a: Automatic activation happens in everyone; it does not set low-prejudiced people apart, since they go on to override it.
wrong.c: Contradictory: controlled processing cannot produce involuntary stereotyping.
wrong.d: Contradictory: automatic processing is not voluntary.

q: The term "stream of consciousness", referring to the flow of thoughts in the human mind, was coined by which psychologist?

concept.t: William James described consciousness as a continuous, ever-changing stream of thought rather than a set of separate elements.
He coined the term in Principles of Psychology (1890).

wrong.a: Described the collective unconscious, not the flow of conscious thought.
wrong.b: Analysed consciousness into elements, the opposite of treating it as a continuous stream.
wrong.d: Rejected the study of consciousness altogether.

q: According to Freud, the ___ mind includes accessible memories, which can be recalled at will.
who: Freud's topographical model of the mind

concept.t: Freud's topographical model has three levels: the conscious, the preconscious and the unconscious.
The preconscious holds memories not in awareness right now but recallable at will, like your phone number.

wrong.a: Holds only what is in awareness now, not stored memories waiting to be recalled.
wrong.c: Its contents cannot be recalled at will; they are kept out of awareness by repression.
wrong.d: A principle (every mental event has a cause), not a level of mind.

q: The Mandukya Upanishad describes four states of consciousness (avasthas). The "fourth", pure consciousness beyond waking, dream and deep sleep, is called:

concept.t: The first three avasthas are jagrat (waking), swapna or svapna (dreaming) and sushupti (dreamless deep sleep).
Turiya, literally "the fourth", is the witnessing consciousness present in all three.

wrong.a: The waking state, the first of the four, not the one beyond them.
wrong.b: The dreaming state (also spelt svapna), the second of the four.
wrong.c: Dreamless deep sleep, the third state; turiya is the witness present in it too.

q: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is crucial for:

concept.t: The suprachiasmatic nucleus sits in the hypothalamus, just above the optic chiasm, and is the body's master clock.
Light entrains it through the retinohypothalamic tract, keeping sleep-wake and other daily rhythms in step with day and night.

wrong.a: Depends on the hippocampus, not the SCN.
wrong.c: Depends on Broca's and Wernicke's areas, not the SCN.
wrong.d: Handled by pain pathways such as the spinothalamic tract and somatosensory cortex, not the SCN.

q: In a typical major sleep period, how many cycles of NREM-REM are there?

concept.t: Each NREM-REM cycle lasts about 90 minutes, so seven to eight hours of sleep hold four to six cycles.

wrong.a: Too few for a full night; it would need cycles much longer than 90 minutes.
wrong.c: Six or more would need cycles far shorter than 90 minutes.
wrong.d: Even further off; it would need cycles far shorter than 90 minutes.

q: During a normal night's sleep, how many times do we pass through the different stages of sleep?
who: Standard four to six sleep cycles

concept.t: The standard figure is four to six sleep cycles in a normal night.
No option says 4 to 6 exactly; of the options given, 4 to 7 is the range that contains it.

wrong.a: Far too many; eight or more cycles would not fit a normal night.
wrong.b: Misses part of the usual range: it leaves out four cycles.
wrong.c: Misses part of the usual range: it stops at five and leaves out six.

q: Which of the following characterises slow-wave sleep?
who: Rechtschaffen and Kales staging; N3 since 2007

concept.t: In the older Rechtschaffen and Kales system, stages 3 and 4, dominated by delta waves, were together called slow-wave sleep.
Since 2007 they are merged into a single stage, N3.

wrong.a: Adds stages 1 and 2, which are light sleep, and REM, which has a fast, desynchronised EEG.
wrong.c: Covers all of sleep; REM has a fast, desynchronised EEG and is not slow-wave.
wrong.d: Includes stages 1 and 2, which are light sleep, not slow-wave.

q: Which one of the following characterises somnambulism?

concept.t: Somnambulism is sleepwalking: sitting up, walking or doing complex acts while still asleep.
It is an NREM parasomnia arising from N3, deep slow-wave sleep.

wrong.b: Sleep terrors, marked by fear and screaming rather than walking.
wrong.c: REM sleep behaviour disorder, where the normal muscle paralysis of REM is lost and dreams are acted out.
wrong.d: Restless legs syndrome, a sleep-related movement disorder, not a parasomnia.

q: The main crux of hypnosis is:

concept.t: Hypnosis works through heightened responsiveness to suggestion.
Suggestibility is measured by scales such as the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale.

wrong.a: The analytical faculty is what hypnotic induction quietens, not its basis.
wrong.b: Logical thinking is likewise quietened by induction, not the basis of hypnosis.
wrong.d: Fails because suggestibility is the accepted core of hypnosis.

q: Researchers studying meditation contacted over 10,000 randomly selected adults in 10 nations. Those who meditated regularly were less likely to suffer from stress than adults who meditated less regularly or not at all. Can we conclude that meditation lowers stress? Why?

concept.t: The study is correlational: it measured who meditated and who was stressed, but nobody was randomly assigned to meditate.
Calmer people may meditate more (reverse causation), or a third factor may cause both.
Only an experiment with random assignment can show that meditation causes lower stress.

wrong.a: A large sample improves generalisability, not causal inference.
wrong.b: Random selection improves generalisability, not causal inference; it is not random assignment.
wrong.c: Simply untrue: nobody was randomly assigned to meditate or not.

q: Valium, Xanax, Rohypnol and Halcion are:

concept.t: Valium (diazepam), Xanax (alprazolam), Rohypnol (flunitrazepam) and Halcion (triazolam) all belong to one class: the benzodiazepines.
They do act as sedatives and hypnotics, but the class they share is benzodiazepines.

wrong.b: An older, more dangerous class, such as phenobarbital; these four drugs are not barbiturates.
wrong.c: Describes what they do (calming), not the drug class they share.
wrong.d: Describes another effect (inducing sleep), not their shared class.

q: A man with sleep-onset insomnia is told to lie in bed with the lights off and try as hard as he can to stay awake. This technique is:

concept.t: Paradoxical intention, from Frankl, tells the person to try to do the very thing they fear: here, to stay awake.
It removes the performance anxiety of trying to sleep, so sleep can come on its own.

wrong.b: Re-links the bed with sleep (use the bed only for sleep, get up if awake); a behavioural method from Bootzin.
wrong.c: Limits time in bed to build sleep pressure, then extends it as sleep improves.
wrong.d: Also Frankl's, but turns attention away from the symptom altogether rather than asking the person to pursue it.
